notes: \cpara{States the question: good science needs humility, but of what sort?}
\cpara{First case: the creationist's appeal to humility is ``a very selective underconfidence,'' doubt applied only to an unwelcome conclusion. The post leaves aside whether to call it humility.}
\cpara{Second case, good humility: an engineer who is ``damn sure'' still builds fail-safes, because sure engineers have been wrong before.}

\cpara{Third case, also good: the student who double-checks ``wants to become stronger.'' In the book this post follows ``Tsuyoku Naritai! (I Want To Become Stronger),'' which was written almost four months after it.}
\cpara{Fourth case: the student who never checks because checking cannot bring certainty. The post calls this ``less wise,'' allowing that the feeling behind it may be the same.}

\cpara{Separates ``social modesty,'' which regulates status, from ``scientific humility,'' which you would practice alone in space. The post is open that it uses the word in a narrower sense than the everyday one (``by default they'll associate the words to social modesty''). That social modesty is ``ancestrally relevant'' and scientific humility ``a more recent and rarefied invention'' is asserted without support.}

\clogic{The everyday sense is closer to the student's words than to double-checking. Merriam-Webster defines humility as ``freedom from pride or arrogance,'' and humble as ``not proud or haughty: not arrogant or assertive'' and ``ranking low in a hierarchy or scale.'' What the post calls scientific humility, taking precautions against your own errors, is nearer to what the same dictionary calls prudence: ``caution or circumspection as to danger or risk.'' A proud person can practice it; the post's own engineer is ``damn sure.'' The post keeps the word and leaves out freedom from pride. It closes on the same definition, taken from ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality,'' where our notes make this point again.}
\cpara{The student now cites the problem of induction, and the first reply is about motive (``go home and play video games''). The reasoned reply, the bridge test, comes four paragraphs later.}

\cpara{Argues from physics: because physicists expect their models to work all the time, they follow up small flaws, and rarely a flaw overturns a theory. The closing words, introduced by ``Therefore it is written,'' come from the ninth virtue of the author's own ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality.'' The post does not say whose words they are.}

\cpara{Satire in the voice of an imagined critic: scientists would be better liked if they granted that evolution holds only most of the time, and they ``ought to be more humble, and compromise a little.'' The point is that the demand for this kind of humility is about status, not about getting things right.}

\cpara{Warns that a vaguely understood principle ``can adapt to justify almost any deed.'' The further claim, that people with vague models ``usually end up believing whatever they started out wanting to believe,'' is stated as a general fact without evidence; the study cited two paragraphs later is the nearest support.}

\cpara{Offers the post's test: ask whether the actions a ``humble'' line of thinking recommends make you stronger or weaker. The bridge shows it on a case where extra cables are plainly better than a shrug.}

\cpara{Reports, as the author's own observation (``that I witness''), that most appeals to humility are excuses to shrug, and gives three. The term and its gloss match the cited paper, where Taber and Lodge define disconfirmation bias as spending ``more time and cognitive resources denigrating and counterarguing attitudinally incongruent than congruent arguments.''}

\cpara{Turns to profession: humility, like much religious belief, is easy to profess. It credits Daniel Dennett with ``belief in belief'' and with the proposal to study religious ``profession.'' As in our notes on ``Belief in Belief,'' I could not check these against Dennett's book.}
\cpara{Applies this to humility: ``Well, of course I could be wrong'' acknowledges doubt and changes nothing.}
\cpara{Names the temptation to change beliefs and actions as little as possible, and quotes John Kenneth Galbraith on getting ``busy on the proof.''}

\cpara{Concludes that thinking should shape plans, and that humility, ``properly misunderstood,'' lets new information disappear. It ends by quoting, again as scripture and again without saying whose words they are, the definition of humility from ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality.'' On that definition, see the note on social modesty above.}
